title: Adab of travel
hook: a verse for setting off, company on the road, and praise on the way home

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of guests, and your line: honor the guest. Who did you make room for? Today the courtesy leaves the house with you, and a new week starts on the road. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

The seatbelt clicks. The engine turns over. And before the car pulls out, the driver says a line under her breath, in Arabic. It isn't a line about cars. It comes from the Qur'an, from a passage about riding animals and ships, written long before any engine. Partway through, it admits something. It ends by mentioning a destination that isn't on any map in the car. Today: the manners of leaving home, and of coming back.
screen: `THE SEATBELT CLICKS.` → `A LINE BEFORE PULLING OUT.` → `A DESTINATION NOT ON THE MAP.`

segments.voice: Ibn 'Umar describes it in Sahih Muslim. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, mounted his camel to set out on a journey, he said Allahu akbar three times, and then recited two verses of surah al-Zukhruf. In Pickthall's translation: "Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us, and we were not capable (of subduing them); And lo! unto our Lord we surely are returning." Notice the admission first. We were not capable. The animal, the ship, today the car or the plane: none of it is ours by our own strength. Then the turn at the end. Unto our Lord we are returning. Every trip has a return built into it, and the verse points past the trip to the last return of all. Then he asked, in the same report, for goodness on the journey and for the distance to be made easy. And coming home, he said it again and added: returning, repenting, worshipping, praising our Lord. The adab of travel has two more pieces. Company: a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says, in paraphrase, that if people knew what he knew about traveling alone, no rider would travel alone at night. And home: another hadith in Bukhari calls travel a piece of torment, because it keeps a person from food, drink and sleep. So when your business is done, it says, hurry back to your family. Leave remembering. Travel with others where you can. Come home quickly, praising. It's a whole trip, bracketed by the same remembrance at both ends.
screen: `WE WERE NOT CAPABLE OF IT.` · `UNTO OUR LORD WE ARE RETURNING.` · `NOT ALONE AT NIGHT.` · `DONE? HURRY HOME, PRAISING.`

segments.voice: The practice: say the travel du'a. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the next trip you'll take, even if it's only across town. See yourself sitting down in the seat. If you pray, you can say the words now, in Arabic if you know them, or in English: Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us. If you don't pray, just notice how much of the trip you didn't build: the road, the engine, the hands that made them. Then see yourself arriving home at the end of the day, and walking through your own door. Stay with that return. The bell holds the time.
Adab of travel. The manners of the road: remember Allah setting out, keep company where you can, and come home quickly, praising. Today's word.
Your line: travel remembering. On your next trip, even a short one, say one line as you set off and one as you walk back in. Tomorrow, the adab of sleep. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Muslims setting out on a journey say Allahu akbar and recite the verses of al-Zukhruf, "Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us," in Arabic, and on returning add words of praise.

fork.setup: your trip's business is done a day early. by the hadith, what does the adab of travel suggest?
options: stay on alone and see the sights.
fork.reveal: travel is a piece of torment, the hadith says, keeping a person from food, drink and sleep: when your business is done, hurry home.

original.note: Arabic: journey, travel; a traveler is a musafir.

trapdoor: what you thought: the travel du'a is a prayer for a safe trip.
what it means: a verse that admits we didn't tame the ride ourselves, and remembers that every road ends in a return to our Lord.
what a scholar hears: Ibn 'Umar's report in Sahih Muslim: three takbirs, al-Zukhruf 43:13–14, and on the way back, returning, repenting, worshipping, praising.

sources.quoted: Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us, and we were not capable (of subduing them); And lo! unto our Lord we surely are returning.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1342 (Ibn 'Umar: takbir three times, the verses of al-Zukhruf, and the words on returning)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2998 (if people knew what I know about traveling alone)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1804 (travel is a piece of torment; hurry back to your family)

notes: Pickthall 43:13–14: confirm exact wording and punctuation of the quoted portion.
